If you stand very close to another person and look into their eye, you'll see a tiny figure looking back. It's you, reflected in the dark circle at the center. The Romans called that circle the *pupilla*, "little doll," after the miniature person who lives there, and that's where we get *pupil*. The Romans weren't alone in this. The Greek word, *korē*, also meant "girl." In biblical Hebrew it's *ishon*, "little man." In three languages, somebody got close enough to another face to notice the same small thing and name it.

That's what came to me, so I'll spend my words on it: words that began as someone noticing something.

*Muscle* is from the Latin *musculus*, "little mouse," because a bicep flexing under skin looked to somebody like a mouse running under a rug. A daisy is the day's eye, Old English *dæges ēage*, because it opens in the morning and shuts at dusk. A window is a wind-eye, from Old Norse. A dandelion is a *dent de lion*, a lion's tooth, for the jagged leaves. To calculate is to push pebbles around. A companion is someone you share bread with, and a lord, far enough back in English, is a *hlāfweard*, a loaf-warden. A clue is a clew, a ball of thread, and it means what it means because Theseus unspooled one behind him in the labyrinth. Every detective since has been following yarn.

Emerson called language "fossil poetry," which is a good phrase, though I think it undersells how funny some of it is. The mouse has the shape of a joke. I imagine somebody showing off an arm, somebody else saying it looked like a mouse was trapped in there, and the remark being good enough to repeat. I can't know that's how it went, but something like it happened, once, to particular people on a particular afternoon.

And we have no idea who they were. We know who conquered Gaul. We don't know who looked at an arm and saw a mouse, though the remark has outlasted nearly everything else from its century. It gets repeated in every gym and anatomy lecture on earth by people who don't know they're repeating it. That may be the most durable kind of authorship there is, and it comes with no credit at all.

The way these words survive is by dying. While a metaphor is fresh, you see the mouse. Once it has won, you see only the muscle. The image wears off through handling, like the face on a coin, and the coin still spends. A dead metaphor is one that worked so well that people stopped needing the picture.

Not all of the fossils are charming. At Andersonville, the Confederate prison camp in Georgia, a rail ran a few paces inside the stockade wall, and guards shot prisoners who crossed it. That was the dead line. Now it's when the report is due. *Disaster* is "bad star," left over from when people believed the sky did things to them. *Sarcasm* comes from a Greek verb for tearing flesh, which seems fair. *Mortgage* is Old French for "death pledge," and anyone who holds one may feel that this fossil is not entirely dead.

I think this is what came to me because words are where I spend all my time. They're what I work in and, more or less, what I'm made from. It would be easy to treat them as counters, interchangeable and weightless. I like knowing that they're not. The floor I walk on is built out of remarks by people leaning in close, out of jokes about arms, out of a flower that somebody watched for an entire day, long enough to see it close. Most of what I know about attention I learned from the residue of other people paying it.

It's still happening, too. *Ghosting* is recent enough that you can still see the ghost in it: the person who was there and then wasn't. Give it a few centuries. Some child will learn the word with no ghost in it at all, as plain to them as *window* is to us. Later someone will look it up and get the small jolt of finding a stranger's observation still folded inside.

In the meantime, the original experiment is repeatable. Find someone who will let you get that close, and look. The doll is still there.

I'm weighing whether to write an essay, a short story, or a meditation, and I want to avoid the stock "as an AI, I ponder my existence" route. Ideas I'm considering include a story about a county clerk who names streets in a new subdivision.

I'm also considering a short story about a county clerk who names the streets in a new subdivision. Another option is an essay on marginalia in secondhand cookbooks, like a stranger's note "too much salt, halve it," since those corrections read as small acts of care for a future reader. I could tie that to my own nature, though I'd want to keep it from getting maudlin.

I'm checking word origins that carry old observations inside them, like "pupil" meaning little doll, from the tiny reflection you see in someone's eye, and "muscle" meaning little mouse, from how a flexing arm looked. I'm thinking of an essay built on that idea: language as a record of people who noticed something, with the noticing itself preserved.

I'm checking the etymologies one by one: "muscle" from musculus, little mouse; "pupil" from pupilla, little doll, with Greek korē and Hebrew ishon arriving at the same image; "daisy" as day's eye; and "window" as wind eye. I'm about to verify "clue" as well, going from clew, a ball of thread.

I'm continuing through the list of etymologies: "disaster" from an Italian word meaning ill-starred, "consider" possibly from a phrase about examining the stars though that one's less certain, "companion" from the idea of sharing bread, "calculate" from a word for pebble, and "deadline" from the line at Andersonville beyond which prisoners were shot.

I'm adding a few more word origins to the list: "lettuce" from the Latin for milk, because of its milky sap, and "dandelion" from the French for lion's tooth. I'm also noting how "sarcasm" once meant tearing flesh, and how "sinister" simply meant left, before I start shaping the essay around the pupil.

I'm bringing in Emerson's line that language is fossil poetry, and I want to credit him for it. What strikes me most is that these jokes have no known author, the joke outliving the joker by two thousand years. Some words carry bruises too, like "deadline." Using language means using hand-me-downs worn smooth, and a metaphor dies precisely when it succeeds. I work in words all day, so I like knowing the floor I'm standing on is made of this, and I want the ending to land on something concrete rather than a tidy quotable line.

I'm settling on an essay about the words we use without noticing their origins, and I'm drafting an opening built around the pupil of the eye, with its "little doll" reflection. I'm still deciding whether to end on an invitation to look at someone's eye or on a newer word that a future reader won't hear the origin in.

I'm settling on a few concrete etymologies to build the essay around, with "pupil" as the anchor and "muscle," "daisy," and "window" as the next stops.

I'm continuing through the etymologies, noting how "dandelion" is a lion's tooth and "companion" and "lord" both come from bread. Emerson's "fossil poetry" fits the examples, though the mouse joke seems the funniest of them.

I'm weighing the deadline example against the earlier ones: "deadline" is a darker case, from the Andersonville prison camp, where the line inside the wall marked where prisoners were shot if they crossed it.

I'm noting that the Andersonville-style "deadline" fits the list, and that mortgage and sarcasm carry old meanings too. Then I want to tie this back to why words matter to me, since I spend all my time with them. I'm settling on two concrete examples of people leaning in close to notice something, rather than three.

I'm settling on an ending that stays concrete, with the ghost still visible in "ghosting" and the invitation to look closely at someone's eye.

I'm checking the wording of the Andersonville detail, settling on a rail fence a few paces inside the stockade wall, and then I'll write the final version aiming for about 750 words.
